                    - code [ref=f87e570]: useState

                    - code [ref=f87e572]: setCount

                    - code [ref=f87e578]: useState()

                    - code [ref=f87e579]: setCount()

                    - generic [ref=f87e589]: "function handleClick() {"
                    - generic [ref=f87e590]: setCount(count + 1);
                    - generic [ref=f87e591]: "}"
                    - generic [ref=f87e593]: return (
                    - generic [ref=f87e594]: "<button onClick={handleClick}>"
                    - generic [ref=f87e595]: "Clicked {count} times"
                    - generic [ref=f87e596]: </button>
                    - generic [ref=f87e597]: );
                    - generic [ref=f87e598]: "}"
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e599]:
                    - text: React will call your component function again. This time,
                    - code [ref=f87e600]: count
                    - text: will be
                    - code [ref=f87e601]: "1"
                    - text: . Then it will be
                    - code [ref=f87e602]: "2"
                    - text: . And so on.
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e603]: "If you render the same component multiple times, each will get its own state. Click each button separately:"
                - generic [ref=f87e606]:
                  - generic [ref=f87e607]:
                    - button "App.js" [ref=f87e611] [cursor=pointer]

                    - iframe [ref=f87e639]

                - generic [ref=f87e646]:
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e647]:
                    - text: Notice how each button “remembers” its own
                    - code [ref=f87e648]: count
                    - text: state and doesn’t affect other buttons.
                  - heading "Using Hooks Link for Using Hooks" [level=2] [ref=f87e649]:
                    - text: Using Hooks
                    - link "Link for Using Hooks":
                      - /url: "#using-hooks"
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e650]:
                    - text: Functions starting with
                    - code [ref=f87e651]: use
                    - text: are called
                    - emphasis [ref=f87e652]: Hooks
                    - text: .
                    - code [ref=f87e653]: useState
                    - text: is a built-in Hook provided by React. You can find other built-in Hooks in the
                    - link "API reference." [ref=f87e654] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: /reference/react
                    - text: You can also write your own Hooks by combining the existing ones.
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e655]:
                    - text: Hooks are more restrictive than other functions. You can only call Hooks
                    - emphasis [ref=f87e656]: at the top
                    - text: of your components (or other Hooks). If you want to use
                    - code [ref=f87e657]: useState
                    - text: in a condition or a loop, extract a new component and put it there.
                  - heading "Sharing data between components Link for Sharing data between components" [level=2] [ref=f87e658]:
                    - text: Sharing data between components
                    - link "Link for Sharing data between components":
                      - /url: "#sharing-data-between-components"
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e659]:
                    - text: In the previous example, each
                    - code [ref=f87e660]: MyButton
                    - text: had its own independent
                    - code [ref=f87e661]: count
                    - text: ", and when each button was clicked, only the"
                    - code [ref=f87e662]: count
                    - text: "for the button clicked changed:"
                  - generic [ref=f87e663]:
                    - figure [ref=f87e664]:
                      - img "Diagram showing a tree of three components, one parent labeled MyApp and two children labeled MyButton. Both MyButton components contain a count with value zero." [ref=f87e666]
                      - paragraph [ref=f87e669]:
                        - text: Initially, each
                        - code [ref=f87e670]: MyButton
                        - text: ’s
                        - code [ref=f87e671]: count
                        - text: state is
                        - code [ref=f87e672]: "0"
                    - figure [ref=f87e673]:
                      - img "The same diagram as the previous, with the count of the first child MyButton component highlighted indicating a click with the count value incremented to one. The second MyButton component still contains value zero." [ref=f87e675]
                      - paragraph [ref=f87e678]:
                        - text: The first
                        - code [ref=f87e679]: MyButton
                        - text: updates its
                        - code [ref=f87e680]: count
                        - text: to
                        - code [ref=f87e681]: "1"
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e682]:
                    - text: However, often you’ll need components to
                    - emphasis [ref=f87e683]: share data and always update together
                    - text: .
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e684]:
                    - text: To make both
                    - code [ref=f87e685]: MyButton
                    - text: components display the same
                    - code [ref=f87e686]: count
                    - text: and update together, you need to move the state from the individual buttons “upwards” to the closest component containing all of them.
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e687]:
                    - text: In this example, it is
                    - code [ref=f87e688]: MyApp
                    - text: ":"
                  - generic [ref=f87e689]:
                    - figure [ref=f87e690]:
                      - img "Diagram showing a tree of three components, one parent labeled MyApp and two children labeled MyButton. MyApp contains a count value of zero which is passed down to both of the MyButton components, which also show value zero." [ref=f87e692]
                      - paragraph [ref=f87e695]:
                        - text: Initially,
                        - code [ref=f87e696]: MyApp
                        - text: ’s
                        - code [ref=f87e697]: count
                        - text: state is
                        - code [ref=f87e698]: "0"
                        - text: and is passed down to both children
                    - figure [ref=f87e699]:
                      - img "The same diagram as the previous, with the count of the parent MyApp component highlighted indicating a click with the value incremented to one. The flow to both of the children MyButton components is also highlighted, and the count value in each child is set to one indicating the value was passed down." [ref=f87e701]
                      - paragraph [ref=f87e704]:
                        - text: On click,
                        - code [ref=f87e705]: MyApp
                        - text: updates its
                        - code [ref=f87e706]: count
                        - text: state to
                        - code [ref=f87e707]: "1"
                        - text: and passes it down to both children
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e708]:
                    - text: Now when you click either button, the
                    - code [ref=f87e709]: count
                    - text: in
                    - code [ref=f87e710]: MyApp
                    - text: will change, which will change both of the counts in
                    - code [ref=f87e711]: MyButton
                    - text: . Here’s how you can express this in code.
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e712]:
                    - text: First,
                    - emphasis [ref=f87e713]: move the state up
                    - text: from
                    - code [ref=f87e714]: MyButton
                    - text: into
                    - code [ref=f87e715]: MyApp
                    - text: ":"
                  - code [ref=f87e721]:
                    - generic [ref=f87e722]: "export default function MyApp() {"
                    - generic [ref=f87e723]: const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
                    - generic [ref=f87e725]: "function handleClick() {"
                    - generic [ref=f87e726]: setCount(count + 1);
                    - generic [ref=f87e727]: "}"
                    - generic [ref=f87e729]: return (
                    - generic [ref=f87e730]: <div>
                    - generic [ref=f87e731]: <h1>Counters that update separately</h1>
                    - generic [ref=f87e732]: <MyButton />
                    - generic [ref=f87e733]: <MyButton />
                    - generic [ref=f87e734]: </div>
                    - generic [ref=f87e735]: );
                    - generic [ref=f87e736]: "}"
                    - generic [ref=f87e738]: "function MyButton() {"
                    - generic [ref=f87e739]: // ... we're moving code from here ...
                    - generic [ref=f87e740]: "}"
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e741]:
                    - text: Then,
                    - emphasis [ref=f87e742]: pass the state down
                    - text: from
                    - code [ref=f87e743]: MyApp
                    - text: to each
                    - code [ref=f87e744]: MyButton
                    - text: ", together with the shared click handler. You can pass information to"
                    - code [ref=f87e745]: MyButton
                    - text: using the JSX curly braces, just like you previously did with built-in tags like
                    - code [ref=f87e746]: <img>
                    - text: ":"
                  - code [ref=f87e752]:
                    - generic [ref=f87e753]: "export default function MyApp() {"
                    - generic [ref=f87e754]: const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
                    - generic [ref=f87e756]: "function handleClick() {"
                    - generic [ref=f87e757]: setCount(count + 1);
                    - generic [ref=f87e758]: "}"
                    - generic [ref=f87e760]: return (
                    - generic [ref=f87e761]: <div>
                    - generic [ref=f87e762]: <h1>Counters that update together</h1>
                    - generic [ref=f87e763]: "<MyButton count={count} onClick={handleClick} />"
                    - generic [ref=f87e764]: "<MyButton count={count} onClick={handleClick} />"
                    - generic [ref=f87e765]: </div>
                    - generic [ref=f87e766]: );
                    - generic [ref=f87e767]: "}"
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e768]:
                    - text: The information you pass down like this is called
                    - emphasis [ref=f87e769]: props
                    - text: . Now the
                    - code [ref=f87e770]: MyApp
                    - text: component contains the
                    - code [ref=f87e771]: count
                    - text: state and the
                    - code [ref=f87e772]: handleClick
                    - text: event handler, and
                    - emphasis [ref=f87e773]: passes both of them down as props
                    - text: to each of the buttons.
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e774]:
                    - text: Finally, change
                    - code [ref=f87e775]: MyButton
                    - text: to
                    - emphasis [ref=f87e776]: read
                    - text: "the props you have passed from its parent component:"
                  - code [ref=f87e782]:
                    - generic [ref=f87e783]: "function MyButton({ count, onClick }) {"
                    - generic [ref=f87e784]: return (
                    - generic [ref=f87e785]: "<button onClick={onClick}>"
                    - generic [ref=f87e786]: "Clicked {count} times"
                    - generic [ref=f87e787]: </button>
                    - generic [ref=f87e788]: );
                    - generic [ref=f87e789]: "}"
                  - paragraph [ref=f87e790]:
                    - text: When you click the button, the
                    - code [ref=f87e791]: onClick
                    - text: handler fires. Each button’s
                    - code [ref=f87e792]: onClick
                    - text: prop was set to the
                    - code [ref=f87e793]: handleClick
                    - text: function inside
                    - code [ref=f87e794]: MyApp
                    - text: ", so the code inside of it runs. That code calls"
                    - code [ref=f87e795]: setCount(count + 1)
                    - text: ", incrementing the"
                    - code [ref=f87e796]: count
                    - text: state variable. The new
                    - code [ref=f87e797]: count
                    - text: value is passed as a prop to each button, so they all show the new value. This is called “lifting state up”. By moving state up, you’ve shared it between components.
